blocks.text: A 27-year-old woman presents to the early pregnancy unit with a positive pregnancy test, mild lower abdominal pain and vaginal spotting. Her last menstrual period was approximately six weeks ago. Transvaginal ultrasound shows neither an intrauterine pregnancy nor a definite extrauterine pregnancy.

items.text: Explain the ultrasound finding.
Assess the patient and identify red flags.
Interpret serial β-hCG results.
Outline further investigations and management.
Explain the safety-net advice you would give her.

blocks.text: Pregnancy of unknown location (PUL) is a temporary classification used when a woman has a positive pregnancy test but transvaginal ultrasound does not identify a definite intrauterine pregnancy or a definite extrauterine pregnancy.
It is not a final diagnosis.

blocks.title: The pregnancy may subsequently be identified as:

items.text: A viable intrauterine pregnancy that was too early to visualize.
A non-viable intrauterine pregnancy or resolving pregnancy.
An ectopic pregnancy.
A persistent PUL, in which β-hCG remains detectable but the pregnancy's location is not established.

blocks.text: Critical OSCE point: Every PUL must be followed up until its outcome is established or β-hCG has resolved appropriately. Never assume that an empty uterus means miscarriage or that the patient is safe from ectopic pregnancy.
In a clinical assessment, I would proceed as follows.

items.text: Wash my hands and introduce myself.
Confirm the patient's identity and preferred name.
Explain that I need to ask questions about her symptoms and pregnancy, examine her if necessary, and review her test results.
Obtain consent before any examination or investigation.
Ensure privacy, dignity and a chaperone for intimate examinations.
Assess immediately for haemodynamic instability or evidence of internal bleeding before taking a lengthy history.

blocks.text: A useful opening statement:

"Your pregnancy test is positive, but the ultrasound has not yet shown where the pregnancy is located. This can happen when a pregnancy is very early. However, we must also consider an ectopic pregnancy, which can sometimes be dangerous. I would like to assess your symptoms and arrange the appropriate follow-up."
Use calm, non-judgmental language and acknowledge the patient's concerns, particularly if the pregnancy is wanted or there is uncertainty about its viability.
Use a structured history that prioritizes ectopic pregnancy and rupture.

items.text: Lower abdominal or pelvic pain.
Vaginal bleeding or spotting.
Missed period or positive home pregnancy test.
Dizziness, fainting or collapse.
Shoulder-tip pain, which may indicate diaphragmatic irritation from intra-abdominal bleeding.
Nausea, vomiting, weakness or breathlessness.

blocks.text: Clarify the onset, duration, severity, progression and location of pain. Ask whether it is unilateral, generalized, intermittent or constant.

items.text: First day of the last menstrual period (LMP).
Whether cycles are regular.
Estimated gestational age.
Date of the first positive pregnancy test.
Previous ultrasound findings.
Previous pregnancies, miscarriages, ectopic pregnancies and their treatments.
Previous molar pregnancy.
Whether the pregnancy was conceived spontaneously or through assisted reproduction.

content_groups.group_title: C. Risk factors for ectopic pregnancy

items.text: Previous ectopic pregnancy.
Previous pelvic inflammatory disease or tubal infection.
Previous tubal surgery or sterilization.
Previous ectopic pregnancy treatment with tubal damage.
Infertility and assisted reproductive technology.
Pregnancy occurring with an intrauterine contraceptive device in place.
Smoking.

blocks.text: Important: Many women with ectopic pregnancy have no recognized risk factors.

content_groups.group_title: D. Relevant medical and surgical history

blocks.text: Ask about previous pelvic or abdominal surgery, fertility treatment, current medications, allergies, blood group if known, and any bleeding disorders or anticoagulant use.

content_groups.group_title: E. Example of a focused history

blocks.text: A 27-year-old woman with six weeks of amenorrhoea, mild right iliac fossa pain and scanty vaginal bleeding has a positive pregnancy test. She is haemodynamically stable, with no syncope or shoulder-tip pain. She has no previous ectopic pregnancy.
This history raises suspicion for ectopic pregnancy, but the diagnosis cannot be made from symptoms alone.
Assess the patient's overall condition and vital signs:
Do not be reassured by a normal blood pressure alone. Young patients can compensate for significant blood loss before becoming hypotensive.

items.text: Inspect for distension, scars and visible abnormalities.
Palpate gently for tenderness, particularly in the lower abdomen.
Assess for guarding, rigidity or rebound tenderness.
Look for abdominal distension or signs of peritonism.
Unilateral lower abdominal tenderness may occur with ectopic pregnancy.
Generalized tenderness, guarding or rigidity raises concern for rupture and haemoperitoneum.
A normal abdominal examination does not exclude ectopic pregnancy.

blocks.text: A speculum examination may help establish the source and amount of bleeding and identify cervical lesions or tissue at the cervical os.
A bimanual examination may reveal cervical motion tenderness or adnexal tenderness or a mass. However, these findings are neither sensitive nor specific for ectopic pregnancy.
Do not delay resuscitation or urgent surgical assessment to perform a pelvic examination in an unstable patient.
1. Ectopic pregnancy
Pregnancy implanted outside the uterine cavity, most commonly in the fallopian tube. It must remain a key concern until excluded.
2. Very early intrauterine pregnancy
The pregnancy may be too early to visualize, particularly if ovulation occurred later than expected.
3. Early pregnancy loss
A failing intrauterine pregnancy may have already passed or may be resolving, leaving no identifiable gestational sac.
4. Other causes of pelvic pain
Ovarian cyst, ovarian torsion, pelvic inflammatory disease, urinary tract disease or appendicitis may explain the symptoms, but a positive pregnancy test still requires pregnancy-related assessment.
Measure serum β-hCG and, in a stable patient with PUL, usually repeat it approximately 48 hours later according to the local early-pregnancy protocol.
The purpose is to assess the trend, not to determine the pregnancy's location from a single result.
**Interpreting serial β-hCG**

rows: Repeat clinical assessment and ultrasound at the appropriate interval
Ectopic pregnancy or non-viable pregnancy becomes more concerning
Prompt senior review and further assessment
Continue follow-up until resolution is confirmed
Persistent PUL or ectopic pregnancy remains possible

blocks.text: A viable intrauterine pregnancy does not always follow a single universal rise threshold. The expected increase depends partly on the initial β-hCG concentration. A slow rise is concerning, but β-hCG trends alone cannot reliably distinguish ectopic pregnancy from intrauterine pregnancy loss.
Similarly, a falling β-hCG does not completely eliminate the risk of ectopic rupture.
TVUS is the preferred imaging method for locating an early pregnancy.

blocks.title: The sonographer or clinician should assess:

items.text: The uterine cavity for a gestational sac, yolk sac and embryo.
Both adnexa for an extrauterine gestational sac or suspicious mass.
The ovaries and any adnexal lesions.
The pelvis for free fluid, especially fluid suggestive of haemoperitoneum.

blocks.text: **Important ultrasound interpretations**
Definite intrauterine pregnancy

An intrauterine gestational sac containing a yolk sac or embryo confirms an intrauterine pregnancy in the usual clinical setting. Heterotopic pregnancy remains possible, particularly after assisted reproduction.
Pregnancy of unknown location
No definite intrauterine or extrauterine pregnancy is seen. Arrange structured follow-up based on symptoms, β-hCG and the ultrasound findings.
Suspicious for ectopic pregnancy
An extrauterine gestational sac, an adnexal mass separate from the ovary, or significant free fluid may raise suspicion. Interpret the findings in the clinical context.

items.text: Full blood count (FBC): assess haemoglobin and baseline blood counts.
Blood group, Rh status and antibody screen; arrange group and save or crossmatch if bleeding is significant.
Urea, electrolytes and renal function if clinically indicated or before certain treatments.
Liver function tests when considering methotrexate.
Urinalysis where urinary symptoms or an alternative diagnosis are suspected.
Other investigations guided by the patient's clinical condition.

blocks.text: If rupture is suspected, blood sampling must not delay resuscitation, urgent specialist review or surgery.
The discriminatory level is the β-hCG concentration above which an intrauterine gestational sac is expected to be visible on TVUS in many pregnancies.

Some services use a level around 1,500–2,000 IU/L, while a more conservative threshold, sometimes up to approximately 3,500 IU/L, may be used when avoiding interruption of a potentially viable pregnancy is especially important.

However, there is no absolute discriminatory value that independently diagnoses ectopic pregnancy. Visibility depends on factors such as equipment, operator expertise, multiple gestation and dating accuracy.

items.text: β-hCG of 800 IU/L with an empty uterus: an early intrauterine pregnancy remains possible.
β-hCG of 2,000 IU/L with an empty uterus: concern increases, but the finding is not diagnostic.
β-hCG of 4,000 IU/L with no intrauterine pregnancy: requires prompt expert review and repeat assessment, but treatment should not be based on this result alone in a stable patient.

blocks.text: The critical question is not simply, "Is the β-hCG above the discriminatory level?" It is, "What combination of symptoms, serial β-hCG and expert ultrasound findings best establishes the diagnosis without risking a viable pregnancy?"
Management depends on haemodynamic stability, symptoms, β-hCG trends, ultrasound findings, follow-up reliability and the patient's preferences.

content_groups.group_title: A. If the patient is haemodynamically unstable

blocks.text: Suspect ruptured ectopic pregnancy or significant intra-abdominal bleeding if there is severe pain, syncope, hypotension, tachycardia or peritonism.

items.text: Call for immediate senior obstetric/gynaecological and anaesthetic assistance.
Initiate ABCDE assessment and resuscitation.
Establish large-bore IV access and obtain urgent blood tests and crossmatch.
Give appropriate IV fluids and blood products according to clinical need.
Arrange emergency operative management when indicated.

blocks.text: Do not wait for serial β-hCG measurements or a repeat ultrasound if the patient is clinically unstable and rupture is suspected.

content_groups.group_title: B. If the patient is stable

items.text: Review the history, examination, quantitative β-hCG and TVUS findings together.
Arrange repeat β-hCG, usually after 48 hours, and repeat ultrasound based on the trend and clinical findings.
Provide written safety-net instructions and a clear follow-up plan.
Escalate promptly if symptoms worsen, β-hCG plateaus or rises abnormally, or ultrasound becomes suspicious for ectopic pregnancy.

content_groups.group_title: C. Management according to the eventual diagnosis

rows: Follow-up ultrasound to establish location and viability
Follow β-hCG to an appropriately negative result, or use an accepted local protocol
Expectant, medical or surgical management according to eligibility and clinical circumstances
Specialist review; further investigations and possible treatment based on the overall findings

blocks.text: Expectant management may be appropriate for carefully selected stable patients with low or declining β-hCG and no concerning clinical findings. Methotrexate may be considered for a confirmed or sufficiently established ectopic pregnancy when eligibility criteria are met and a viable intrauterine pregnancy has been excluded. Surgery is required for many ruptured ectopic pregnancies and other cases where conservative treatment is unsuitable.
Do not give methotrexate merely because the uterus is empty on ultrasound.

subsections.subsection_title: 10. Safety-net advice — a crucial OSCE component

blocks.text: Explain that the pregnancy's location is not yet known and that ectopic pregnancy can occasionally cause serious bleeding even when β-hCG is low or falling.

blocks.title: Tell the patient to attend the emergency department immediately if she develops:

items.text: Severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain.
Shoulder-tip pain.
Dizziness, fainting or collapse.
Heavy vaginal bleeding.
Marked weakness, breathlessness or feeling acutely unwell.

blocks.text: She must attend scheduled blood tests and ultrasound appointments even if the pain and bleeding stop.
If she cannot reliably attend follow-up or access emergency care, this should influence the management plan and may justify a more closely supervised approach.

subsections.subsection_title: 11. How to report your findings in the OSCE

content_groups.group_title: Example A: Stable patient with PUL

blocks.text: "This is a haemodynamically stable woman with a positive pregnancy test and early pregnancy symptoms. Transvaginal ultrasound has not identified a definite intrauterine or extrauterine pregnancy, so the current classification is pregnancy of unknown location. Ectopic pregnancy has not been excluded. I would correlate the findings with quantitative serum β-hCG, arrange repeat measurement after approximately 48 hours and plan further ultrasound and specialist review according to the clinical findings. I would provide explicit ectopic pregnancy safety-net advice."

content_groups.group_title: Example B: PUL with concerning symptoms

blocks.text: "This patient has a positive pregnancy test, unilateral lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. In view of the symptoms, ectopic pregnancy is a major differential diagnosis. I would urgently reassess her haemodynamic status, request senior gynaecological review and arrange appropriate investigations. If there is evidence of rupture or circulatory compromise, I would initiate resuscitation and arrange emergency operative management without delay."

"The falling β-hCG suggests a resolving pregnancy; however, because the pregnancy location has not been established, ectopic pregnancy cannot yet be excluded. I would continue follow-up until resolution is confirmed according to the local protocol and advise immediate reassessment if symptoms develop or worsen."

subsections.subsection_title: 12. Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is pregnancy of unknown location?
It is a positive pregnancy test with no definite intrauterine or extrauterine pregnancy identified on transvaginal ultrasound. It is a temporary classification rather than a definitive diagnosis.
Q2. What are the main possible outcomes of PUL?
A subsequently identified intrauterine pregnancy, a resolving pregnancy, an ectopic pregnancy or persistent PUL.
Q3. Can a single β-hCG value diagnose ectopic pregnancy?
No. It must be interpreted with the clinical presentation, serial measurements and ultrasound findings.
Q4. What does a plateauing β-hCG suggest?
It raises concern for ectopic pregnancy or persistent trophoblastic tissue, including a non-viable intrauterine pregnancy. Further assessment is required.
Q5. Can a falling β-hCG exclude ectopic pregnancy?
No. Ectopic pregnancies can have falling β-hCG levels and may still rupture.
Q6. What is the most appropriate imaging investigation?
Transvaginal ultrasound, performed and interpreted in the context of the clinical presentation.
Q7. When should methotrexate be avoided?

It should not be given solely for an empty uterus or an indeterminate scan. A potentially viable intrauterine pregnancy must be excluded, and the patient must meet the relevant eligibility criteria. Significant contraindications include breastfeeding, important renal or hepatic dysfunction, clinically significant blood dyscrasias and immunodeficiency. The full local protocol must be checked.
Q8. What is the most important discharge instruction?
Attend all planned follow-up and seek emergency care immediately for severe or worsening pain, shoulder-tip pain, fainting, collapse or heavy bleeding.
Q9. Why is an empty uterus not sufficient to diagnose ectopic pregnancy?
The pregnancy may be too early to visualize, or it may have already resolved. An empty uterus alone does not establish the pregnancy's location.
Q10. What is a heterotopic pregnancy?
The simultaneous presence of an intrauterine pregnancy and an ectopic pregnancy. It is uncommon after spontaneous conception but more frequent after assisted reproductive treatment.

items.text: Calling PUL an ectopic pregnancy without sufficient evidence.
Assuming an empty uterus confirms miscarriage.
Using a single β-hCG value to decide that a pregnancy is non-viable.
Discharging a symptomatic patient without a documented follow-up plan.
Assuming falling β-hCG means there is no risk of rupture.
Administering methotrexate before adequately excluding a viable intrauterine pregnancy.
Delaying emergency treatment in a patient with suspected rupture.
Forgetting to explain warning symptoms in language the patient understands.

blocks.text: Pregnancy test — confirm pregnancy and obtain quantitative β-hCG.
Recognize red flags — pain, syncope, shoulder-tip pain and haemodynamic instability.
Examine — assess vital signs and abdominal findings.
Gynaecological ultrasound — assess the uterus, adnexa and free fluid.
Next β-hCG — arrange serial measurement when appropriate.
Assess the trend — interpret β-hCG alongside symptoms and imaging.
Never miss ectopic pregnancy — maintain suspicion until the outcome is established.
Counsel — explain uncertainty and provide safety-net advice.
Your follow-up plan — ensure documented review until resolution or diagnosis.
**The three rules to remember**

items.text: Unstable patient: resuscitate and urgently involve the gynaecology team.
Stable patient: combine symptoms, serial β-hCG and ultrasound findings.
Undiagnosed pregnancy: never abandon follow-up until the outcome is established.

blocks.text: 1. A woman has a positive pregnancy test, β-hCG of 900 IU/L and an empty uterus on TVUS. What is the correct classification?
Confirmed ectopic pregnancy
Pregnancy of unknown location
Confirmed miscarriage
Molar pregnancy
2. A patient with PUL develops severe abdominal pain, tachycardia and hypotension. What is the priority?
Repeat β-hCG in 48 hours
Discharge with outpatient follow-up
Immediate resuscitation and urgent gynaecological assessment
Give methotrexate immediately
3. Her β-hCG falls substantially over 48 hours. What should you conclude?
Ectopic pregnancy is excluded
The pregnancy is definitely intrauterine
The pregnancy may be resolving, but ectopic pregnancy is not excluded
No further follow-up is needed
4. Which finding definitively establishes a usual intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound?
An empty uterus
A thickened endometrium
An intrauterine gestational sac containing a yolk sac or embryo
A single elevated β-hCG
